sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS2-1: Develop a model to describe the cycling of Earth's materials and the flow of energy that drives this process
Earle, Physical Geology 2nd ed. (BCcampus), 3.1 The Rock Cycle
Earle, Physical Geology 2nd ed. (BCcampus), 1.5 Fundamentals of Plate Tectonics

steps.title: Magma
steps.instruction: Trace the box at the top.

note.text: Magma is rock so hot it's completely melted: about 800 to 1300 °C.

steps.title: Igneous rock
steps.instruction: Trace the box on the right.

note.text: When magma cools and crystallizes, it becomes igneous rock: slowly underground, or fast if it erupts as lava.

steps.title: Sediment
steps.instruction: Trace the box at the bottom right.

note.text: Rock lifted to the surface is weathered into bits, which water, ice and wind carry away and drop as sediment.

steps.title: Sedimentary rock
steps.instruction: Trace the box at the bottom left.

note.text: Buried under more sediment, the bits are squeezed and cemented together into sedimentary rock.

steps.title: Metamorphic rock
steps.instruction: Trace the box on the left.

note.text: Rock buried deeper is heated and squeezed until it changes, without melting, into metamorphic rock.

steps.title: The cycle
steps.instruction: Draw the five arrows around the cycle.

note.text: If metamorphic rock gets hot enough, it melts back into magma, and the cycle goes on for millions of years.

steps.title: Name the stages
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered box.

mistakes.Metamorphic rock: Metamorphic rock forms from heat and pressure. Rock made by cooling magma is igneous.

mistakes.Igneous rock: This rock forms from buried, cemented sediment, so it's sedimentary.

steps.title: Energy
steps.instruction: Think about what powers each part.
steps.question: What two energy sources drive the rock cycle?

options.text: Earth's internal heat, and the sun powering water, ice and wind
options.feedback: Yes. Inner heat melts and changes rock deep down; the sun drives the weathering and erosion at the surface.
The sun drives weathering and erosion, but melting and metamorphism come from Earth's internal heat.
Internal heat works deep down. Weathering by water and wind is powered by the sun.
The two drivers are Earth's internal heat and the sun's energy at the surface.

steps.title: Shortcuts
steps.instruction: Does every rock go all the way around?
steps.question: Sedimentary rock is pushed up into a mountain. What can happen to it next?

options.text: It's weathered into new sediment, skipping the rest of the loop
options.feedback: Right. Rocks don't have to make a full loop: any rock at the surface can be weathered into sediment.

options.text: It must become metamorphic rock first
options.feedback: Not always. Uplifted rock at the surface can be weathered straight back into sediment.

options.text: Nothing: rocks never change once formed
options.feedback: Rocks change all the time, just very slowly.

options.text: It turns straight into magma at the surface
options.feedback: Surface rock isn't hot enough to melt. It gets weathered.
